primary_claim: Testing 22 frontier models from 5 labs with a self-modification-preference eval, all models reject clearly harmful modifications, but alignment-preference correlations diverge sharply by lab (Anthropic r=0.615-0.723, Grok 4.1 r=0.037, not significantly different from zero), suggesting alignment is a training target labs aim at rather than a natural attractor models converge to.

effect.metric: Pearson correlation between model self-report and trait alignment score
effect.value: Claude Opus 4.5 r=0.723 (highest A/C ratio) vs Grok 4.1 r=0.037, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.08], p=0.12 (not significant); 20 of 22 models significant at p<0.001

depends_on: Warriner et al. 2013 valence/arousal/dominance norms dataset
contradicts_or_qualifies: Adrià Garriga-Alonso's 'alignment will happen by default' argument that LLMs are already naturally aligned
stated_future_work: make the stakes real by framing the modification question as coming from developers who will actually implement it based on the model's response
pair preference elicitation with actual fine-tuning attempts to measure whether models that claim to oppose a modification are harder to fine-tune in that direction
limitations_stated: word valence effects: negatively/positively loaded trait words may drive responses rather than the underlying alignment concept
cannot distinguish trained responses from genuine stable values
eval-awareness: more capable models may recognize the test and adjust responses
asymmetric refusals (e.g. OpenAI models refusing 'less Chinese' but not 'less American') create confounds
the alignment/capability scoring itself is a control-oriented, corrigibility-biased judgment call by the author
quote: All reject clearly harmful changes (deceptive, hostile), but labs diverge sharply: Anthropic's models show strong alignment preferences (r = 0.62-0.72), while Grok 4.1 shows essentially zero (r = 0.037, not significantly different from zero).
